intro: Every copy of the Tanakh you can hold is the end of a chain. A scribe copied it from a copy, which was copied from a copy, back through printing presses in Venice, codices in Tiberias and Cairo, scrolls in caves by the Dead Sea, and manuscripts nobody has seen for two thousand years. Along the way the text was translated into Greek, Aramaic, Latin, German and English, and each translation made choices the reader cannot see. This unit follows that chain link by link.

The questions are practical ones that any careful reader can ask. What did the oldest copies say, and how do we know? Who added the vowels to a text written in consonants? Why does the Greek Jeremiah differ from the Hebrew? What did the JPS committee of 1917 decide about Isaiah 7:14, and why did the King James decide otherwise? What happens to a word like chesed when it becomes mercy? Jewish tradition holds the text as received; historians trace how it was received; translators sit in between. This unit lets you hear all three.

By the end you will be able to name the main witnesses to the Hebrew text and place them in order, explain what the Masoretes did and why it mattered, read a famous variant and weigh it, set two translations of one verse side by side and say what each translator chose, and explain why Jews write the LORD for the name of God. You will also have a habit: when you read a verse in English, you will ask who translated it, when, for whom, and from what.
bigQuestion: How did the words of the Tanakh reach us, and what does it mean to read them in translation?

title: Text, Transmission and Translation

chapters.title: From Scroll to Codex: Masoretes, Scrolls and Versions
chapters.bigQuestion: How did the words of the Tanakh travel across two thousand years of copying, and how do we know what the oldest copies said?

story.title: A Stone, a Jar and a Cave
story.kicker: In the winter of 1946–47 a young shepherd near the Dead Sea threw a stone into a dark opening in the cliff and heard something break.
paragraphs: The hills above the Dead Sea are dry, pale and full of holes. In the winter of 1946–47, as the story is usually told, a young Bedouin shepherd named Muhammad edh-Dhib was searching for a lost animal near the ruins of Qumran. He tossed a stone into an opening in the rock. Instead of the click of stone on stone, he heard the crack of pottery. Something was inside.

When he and his companions climbed in, they found tall clay jars. Some were empty. Others held rolls of leather wrapped in linen. The rolls were covered in Hebrew letters. The shepherds did not know what they had, but they knew old things could be sold. Within a year the rolls had passed through a Bethlehem dealer's shop and into the hands of scholars in Jerusalem, who slowly understood what they were looking at.

One roll was a complete copy of the book of Isaiah, all sixty-six chapters, on seventeen sheets of leather sewn end to end. Scholars later dated it to around 125 BCE. Before that day, the oldest complete Hebrew copies of Isaiah anyone had were about a thousand years younger. Now a reader could set the two side by side and ask a question that had waited for centuries: how much had changed in a thousand years of copying?

The answer surprised many people. The old scroll and the medieval codex were, for the most part, the same book. Spellings differed. A word was missing here, added there. A handful of verses read differently in ways scholars still discuss. But the story of how the Tanakh's text was carried forward, letter by letter, could now be told with evidence in hand. This chapter tells that story, from the caves to the printed page.
story.think: If you found a book a thousand years older than any other copy, what would you compare first, and what would count as a big difference?

lessons.title: The Find at Qumran
lessons.mainIdea: The Dead Sea Scrolls, found from 1947 on in caves near Qumran, are the oldest known manuscripts of books of the Tanakh.
reading: The *Dead Sea Scrolls* are a collection of ancient manuscripts found in eleven caves near *Qumran*, on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea, beginning in 1947. Over the following decade, Bedouin searchers and archaeologists recovered fragments of roughly nine hundred separate manuscripts. Most are small pieces, some no bigger than a fingernail. A few are nearly whole scrolls.

About a quarter of the scrolls are copies of books of the Tanakh. Scholars have identified fragments of every book except Esther. The rest are other writings: prayers, rules for a community, commentaries on prophets, and books later left out of the Jewish canon. Most are in Hebrew, some in Aramaic, and a few in Greek. Scholars date them, by handwriting and by carbon testing, from about the third century BCE to the first century CE.

Who put them there is still debated. Many scholars connect the scrolls with a Jewish group that lived at Qumran, often identified with the Essenes described by the ancient writers Josephus and Pliny. Others argue the caves held books brought from Jerusalem for safety before the Roman war of 66–70 CE. Either way, the scrolls give readers a window into the text of the Tanakh a thousand years before the oldest complete Hebrew Bibles that survived elsewhere.

a ruined settlement on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea, near the caves where the scrolls were found

lessons.title: The Great Isaiah Scroll
lessons.mainIdea: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Cave 1, copied around 125 BCE, is the oldest complete copy of any book of the Tanakh.
reading: The best-known scroll from Cave 1 is the *Great Isaiah Scroll*, which scholars label 1QIsa-a. It holds the whole book of Isaiah, all sixty-six chapters, written in fifty-four columns on seventeen sheets of leather sewn together. Unrolled, it is about 7.3 meters long, roughly the length of a school bus's front half. Scholars date the copying to about 125 BCE, give or take a few decades.

What does the scroll show? First, that the book of Isaiah already had the shape it has today more than two thousand years ago. Chapters 1 to 39 and chapters 40 to 66, which many modern scholars think come from different times, sit together on one scroll with only a small gap. Second, that the text was already very close to the one Jews read now. A reader who knows the medieval Hebrew text can read this scroll without much trouble.

The differences are real but mostly small. The scroll uses more vowel-letters, extra letters that hint at pronunciation, so many words are spelled longer. Some words are switched or dropped. In a few places the wording differs in ways readers care about. Isaiah 53:11, for example, includes the word light, so the servant sees light, where the later standard text has no object for the verb. Scholars weigh such cases one at a time.

Today the scroll is kept at the Shrine of the Book, part of the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, and a high-resolution image of it can be studied online. Jewish tradition does not treat the scroll as a rival to the received text. It plays no role in the synagogue. For historians, though, it is the most important witness to how a prophetic book looked in the late Second Temple period.

words.d: the complete copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 1 (1QIsa-a), dated to about 125 BCE
one block of writing on a scroll, read from top to bottom before moving left to the next
a Hebrew consonant used to hint at a vowel sound, so a word is spelled with more letters
any manuscript or version that shows what a text said at some point in its history

lessons.title: What a Thousand Years Changed
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing the scrolls with the medieval text shows a very stable tradition with a small number of real variants worth studying.
reading: Put the Great Isaiah Scroll beside a printed Hebrew Bible and the first lesson is stability. Over roughly eleven centuries, from about 125 BCE to the Aleppo Codex around 930 CE, copyists carried the book of Isaiah forward with remarkable care. Scholars who count every difference find that the great majority are spelling, and most of the rest do not change the meaning. This is why the Qumran finds strengthened, rather than shook, confidence in the received Hebrew text.

The second lesson is that the text was not frozen. Other Qumran scrolls show more variety than the Isaiah scroll. Some copies of Jeremiah are close to the Hebrew text we have; others are shorter and ordered differently, like the Greek Septuagint. A copy of Samuel from Cave 4 preserves lines about King Nahash of Ammon that the received text lacks. A Psalms scroll from Cave 11 orders the psalms differently and includes songs not in the book of Psalms.

Scholars describe this period as one of textual plurality: several forms of some books circulated side by side. By about the second century CE, one form, the ancestor of the *Masoretic Text*, had become the standard among Jews. The Masoretic Text, or MT, is the Hebrew text as fixed and annotated by the Masoretes of the early Middle Ages, and it is the text every synagogue scroll and every Jewish translation follows. Jewish tradition holds this text as authoritative; historians study how it came to be so.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Tanakh as fixed and annotated by the Masoretes; abbreviated MT
the situation, seen at Qumran, in which more than one form of a biblical book circulated at the same time
a place where two manuscripts or versions of the same text read differently

look.title: The Missing Line in Psalm 145
look.text: Psalm 145 is an alphabet poem: each verse begins with the next Hebrew letter. In the Masoretic Text one letter, nun, has no verse. The Psalms scroll from Qumran Cave 11 and the Greek Septuagint both have a nun verse, roughly: The LORD is faithful in all His words, and gracious in all His works. Some scholars think the line fell out by accident in one early copy; some rabbinic readers explained the gap as deliberate. Modern Jewish prayer books follow the Masoretic Text and leave the line out.
look.prompt: Which explanation would you find more convincing, and what evidence would settle it? Why might a prayer book keep the received text even so?

The medieval text was translated back from Greek
The book of Isaiah was still being written at Qumran
check.why: The comparison showed a stable tradition; most differences are spelling, and only a few verses differ in ways that change meaning.

check.why: Textual plurality describes the Second Temple situation in which several forms of some books, such as Jeremiah, existed side by side.

check.why: The Cave 11 Psalms scroll (11QPs-a) differs in order and content; the Samuel scroll is known for the Nahash lines and the Isaiah scroll for its completeness.

lessons.title: The Septuagint
lessons.mainIdea: The Septuagint is the Greek translation of the Tanakh made in Egypt from about the third century BCE, the first translation of the Bible into any language.
reading: By the third century BCE many Jews lived in Alexandria, the Greek-speaking capital of Egypt, and fewer and fewer of them could read Hebrew. In that setting the Torah was translated into Greek. Tradition dates the work to the reign of Ptolemy II, around 250 BCE. The other books followed over the next century or two. The whole is called the *Septuagint*, from the Latin for seventy, and is often written with the Roman numeral LXX.

The name comes from a legend told in the *Letter of Aristeas*, a Greek text from perhaps the second century BCE. It says King Ptolemy asked the high priest in Jerusalem for scholars, and seventy-two elders came, six from each tribe, and produced the translation for the royal library. Later tellings, in Philo and in the Talmud, add that the translators worked separately and yet agreed word for word. Historians read the letter as a story told to honor the translation, not a report.

The Septuagint mattered enormously. It was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews for centuries, and it became the Old Testament of the early Christian church. When the New Testament quotes Scripture, it usually quotes the Greek. Over time, as Christians adopted the Septuagint, Jewish communities returned to the Hebrew, and new Greek translations closer to the Hebrew were made by Jewish translators such as Aquila in the second century CE.

For students of the text, the Septuagint is a witness in its own right. Because the translators worked from Hebrew manuscripts older than any we have, their Greek sometimes shows what their Hebrew said. Where the Greek differs from the Masoretic Text, a scholar asks: did the translator have a different Hebrew, misread it, or choose to interpret? The Qumran scrolls often help answer, since some of them agree with the Greek against the later Hebrew.

words.d: the ancient Greek translation of the Tanakh, begun in Alexandria around the third century BCE; abbreviated LXX
a Greek text of about the second century BCE that tells the legend of seventy-two translators producing the Greek Torah
the Greek-speaking capital of Ptolemaic Egypt, home to a large Jewish community
a Jewish translator of the second century CE who made a very literal Greek version of the Hebrew Bible

look.title: Seventy-Two Elders
look.text: The Letter of Aristeas tells that King Ptolemy of Egypt wrote to Eleazar the high priest in Jerusalem, asking for learned men to translate the Jewish law into Greek for the royal library. Eleazar chose seventy-two elders, six from each tribe, and sent them with a copy of the law written in gold letters. They worked on an island near the harbor and finished in seventy-two days, and the Jews of Alexandria gathered to hear the translation read and approved it.
look.cite: Letter of Aristeas, sections 32–47 and 301–311, summarized from the English translation of H. T. Andrews in R. H. Charles, The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament (1913)
look.prompt: What does the story want its readers to believe about the translation? Which details do that work?

lessons.title: Where the Greek Differs
lessons.mainIdea: The Septuagint differs from the Hebrew in the length and order of some books, in numbering, in which books it includes and in particular readings.
reading: Anyone who reads Jeremiah in Greek and in Hebrew notices at once that they are not the same size. The Greek Jeremiah is about one-eighth shorter, and the oracles against foreign nations, which come at the end of the Hebrew book, sit in the middle of the Greek one. Fragments of Jeremiah from Qumran Cave 4 show that a shorter Hebrew form once existed too. Many scholars think the Greek translates an earlier edition of the book and the Hebrew a later, expanded one.

The Septuagint also numbers the Psalms differently, joining and splitting a few. From Psalm 10 to Psalm 147 the Greek number is one lower than the Hebrew. Catholic Bibles long followed the Greek numbering; Jewish and Protestant Bibles follow the Hebrew. The Greek collection also holds books outside the Jewish canon. Among them are Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, the Wisdom of Solomon and Ben Sira, and longer forms of Esther and Daniel.

Then there are single words. The most discussed is Isaiah 7:14. The Hebrew word *almah* means a young woman of marriageable age. The Septuagint rendered it with the Greek *parthenos*, which usually means virgin. The Gospel of Matthew quotes the Greek. Jewish translations render the Hebrew: the JPS 1917 says the young woman, and so does the NJPS. Christian translations divide; the King James says a virgin, while several modern Christian versions say young woman with a note. The next chapter returns to this verse.

the Greek word, usually meaning virgin, that the Septuagint used at Isaiah 7:14
the list of books a community accepts as its Scripture
a distinct form of a book, such as the shorter Jeremiah behind the Greek and the longer one in the Hebrew

lessons.title: Targums and the Samaritan Torah
lessons.mainIdea: The Aramaic Targums and the Samaritan Pentateuch are two more ancient forms of the text, each shaped by the community that used it.
reading: After the Babylonian exile, many Jews spoke *Aramaic*, a language close to Hebrew and the common tongue of the Persian Empire. When the Torah was read aloud in synagogue, a translator would render each verse into Aramaic so that everyone could follow. These spoken translations were eventually written down as the *Targums*, from the Aramaic word for translation. The Mishnah already describes the practice: one verse of Torah, then its translation, verse by verse.

The best-known Targums are Targum Onkelos on the Torah and Targum Jonathan on the Prophets, both edited into their present form in Babylonia by about the fourth or fifth century CE. Onkelos stays close to the Hebrew but softens language that gives God a body. Where the Hebrew says God's hand or God's anger, Onkelos often speaks of God's word or God's presence. Rashi cites Onkelos constantly, and traditional printed Bibles set it beside the Hebrew.

The *Samaritan Pentateuch* is different in kind. The Samaritans are a community, still living today near Nablus and in Holon, who hold only the five books of Moses as Scripture and worship on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. Their Torah, written in an older Hebrew script, differs from the Masoretic Text in about six thousand places. Most are spelling and grammar. Some agree with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text, which suggests an old shared source.

A few Samaritan readings reflect the community's beliefs. In Deuteronomy 27:4 the Masoretic Text says the altar is to be built on Mount Ebal; the Samaritan text says Mount Gerizim. The Samaritan version of the Ten Commandments adds a commandment to build that altar on Gerizim. Scholars debate which reading is older in each case. What is not in doubt is that a community's text and a community's practice shaped each other, as they did for Jews, Christians and Samaritans alike.

words.d: a language close to Hebrew, widely spoken by Jews after the Babylonian exile; the language of the Targums and parts of Daniel and Ezra
an Aramaic translation of a book of the Tanakh, grown from verse-by-verse translation in the synagogue
the standard Aramaic Targum on the Torah, edited in Babylonia and printed beside the Hebrew in traditional Bibles
the Torah as kept by the Samaritan community, in an older Hebrew script, with about six thousand differences from the Masoretic Text

look.title: Ebal or Gerizim?
look.text: Deuteronomy 27:4 in the Masoretic Text: when you cross the Jordan, set up these stones on Mount Ebal. The same verse in the Samaritan Pentateuch: set up these stones on Mount Gerizim. Gerizim is the Samaritans' holy mountain to this day. Ebal is the mountain of the curses in Deuteronomy 27:13. One reading has a clear reason to exist if it was changed; the other seems odd, since Deuteronomy blesses from Gerizim, not Ebal.
look.prompt: A rule of textual study says the harder reading is often older, because copyists smooth, not roughen. Apply that rule here. Then say why it might not settle the question.

check.q: What is a Targum?
choices: A Greek translation of the Torah made in Egypt
A list of the books in the canon
A scroll written in the old Hebrew script
An Aramaic translation of a biblical book that began as spoken synagogue translation
check.why: Targums are Aramaic translations that grew from the practice of translating each verse aloud in synagogue.

check.q: How does Targum Onkelos often handle language that gives God a body?
choices: It softens it, speaking of God's word or presence
It adds a note that the language is literal

lessons.title: Vowels and Accents
lessons.mainIdea: The Masoretes of Tiberias, between about the seventh and tenth centuries CE, added vowel points and accent marks to a text that had been written in consonants alone.
reading: Hebrew is written with consonants. A Torah scroll today, like the scrolls at Qumran, has no vowels at all. A reader who knows the language supplies them, the way an English reader can read a sign that says PLS CLS DR. But two words can share consonants and differ in vowels, and a text read in public across many communities needs a fixed pronunciation. The *Masoretes* met that need.

The Masoretes were families of Jewish scholars, most famously in *Tiberias* on the Sea of Galilee, who worked from about the seventh to the tenth century CE. Their name comes from *masorah*, tradition, the handing-down of the text. They devised a system of dots and dashes, the vowel points, written above, below and inside the consonants, that fixed how every word is read. A related system of marks, the *cantillation* accents, fixed how the verse is chanted and where its phrases break.

Two families of Tiberian Masoretes, Ben Asher and Ben Naphtali, differed in small details. The text of Aaron ben Asher, of the early tenth century, became the standard. Maimonides, writing in the twelfth century, praised a codex checked by Ben Asher as the model he used for his own Torah scroll. Other systems of vowel marks, from Babylonia and from the Land of Israel, were used for a time and then fell out of use.

The Masoretes did not invent the pronunciation; they recorded the reading tradition their communities had inherited. Jewish tradition holds that the reading, like the letters, goes back to Sinai. Historians see in the points a snapshot of how Hebrew was read in Tiberias around 900 CE. Either way, the points changed the Bible forever. Every printed Hebrew Bible, every translation since the Middle Ages, and every student's first Hebrew lesson rests on the Masoretes' dots.

words.d: Jewish scholars, chiefly of Tiberias, c. 7th–10th centuries CE, who fixed the vowels, accents and notes of the Hebrew text
a city on the Sea of Galilee where the most influential Masoretes worked
Hebrew for tradition or handing-down; the body of notes the Masoretes wrote to guard the text
the dots and dashes added to Hebrew consonants to fix how each word is read
the system of accent marks that shows how a verse is chanted and where its phrases divide

lessons.title: Counting Every Letter
lessons.mainIdea: The masorah is a system of notes that counts letters, words and verses so a copyist can check a manuscript against the tradition.
reading: Around the text on the page of a Masoretic codex runs a second text in tiny script: the *masorah*. The notes in the side margins, the masorah parva or small masorah, tell the reader how many times a spelling appears in the Bible. The notes at the top and bottom, the masorah magna or large masorah, list where. At the end of each book stand totals: the number of verses, the middle verse, the number of words and letters.

The point was to make copying checkable. If a scribe knows that a certain word is spelled without a vowel-letter exactly four times in the Torah, and lists where, a wrong spelling stands out. If the count of verses in Genesis comes out wrong, a verse has been dropped or doubled. The Talmud already records scholars who were called counters because they counted every letter of the Torah, and it notes the middle letter, middle word and middle verse of the Torah.

One class of note deserves its own mention: *ketiv* and *qere*, what is written and what is read. In more than a thousand places the Masoretes preserved the consonants of the received text but marked in the margin a different word to be read aloud. Sometimes the ketiv looks like a scribal slip; sometimes the qere avoids a coarse word or a divine name. The scroll keeps the written form; the reader follows the margin. The tradition chose to record both rather than erase either.

words.d: the short notes in the side margin of a Masoretic codex, counting how often a form appears
the longer notes at the top and bottom of the page, listing where each counted form appears
what is written: the consonants of the received text in a place where a different word is read aloud
what is read: the marginal word the reader pronounces instead of the ketiv

lessons.title: Aleppo and Leningrad
lessons.mainIdea: The Aleppo Codex (c. 930 CE) and the Leningrad Codex (1008 CE) are the two most important surviving Masoretic Bibles, and the Leningrad is the basis of modern printed editions.
reading: A scroll is written on one side, unrolled to read, and used in synagogue. A *codex* is a book of pages sewn at the spine, written on both sides, easy to open to any place and to fill with notes. Jews began using the codex for the Bible around the eighth or ninth century CE, keeping the scroll for ritual reading. The great Masoretic codices are the fruit of that change.

The *Aleppo Codex* was written in Tiberias around 930 CE. Its vowels and masorah were added, tradition and most scholars agree, by Aaron ben Asher himself, which made it the most authoritative Hebrew Bible in existence. It passed to Jerusalem, was carried off by Crusaders and ransomed, reached Cairo, where Maimonides is believed to have consulted it, and was kept for six centuries in the great synagogue of Aleppo in Syria. In riots in Aleppo in December 1947, the synagogue was burned. The codex survived, but about a third of its pages, including nearly all the Torah, were lost. What remains is in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

The *Leningrad Codex* was completed in Cairo in 1008 CE by a scribe named Samuel ben Jacob, who says he copied from manuscripts corrected by Ben Asher. It is the oldest complete Masoretic Bible that survives. It came into the collection of Abraham Firkovich and is now in the National Library of Russia in St. Petersburg, keeping the name it acquired when the city was Leningrad. Because it is complete, it became the base text of the standard scholarly edition, the Biblia Hebraica, from 1937 on.

Neither codex is used in synagogue; ritual reading is always from a scroll. But a scribe writing a scroll, a printer setting a Hebrew Bible, or a JPS committee checking a verse all depend on them. The chain of authority runs back through these two books to the Masoretes of Tiberias. Jewish tradition sees in them the careful preservation of a text received. Historians see the earliest complete evidence of the Masoretic achievement.

words.d: a book of pages bound at the spine, as opposed to a scroll
the Masoretic Bible written in Tiberias c. 930 CE, vocalized by Aaron ben Asher, damaged in 1947 and now in Jerusalem
the oldest complete Masoretic Bible, completed in Cairo in 1008 CE and kept in St. Petersburg
the standard scholarly printed edition of the Hebrew Bible, based since 1937 on the Leningrad Codex

lessons.title: Reading a Famous Variant
lessons.mainIdea: Textual criticism compares witnesses to decide which reading is likely earliest, and Deuteronomy 32:8 is a classic case.
reading: *Textual criticism* is the study of a text's witnesses, manuscripts and ancient translations, to work out how the text was transmitted and what its earliest recoverable form said. It is not criticism in the sense of finding fault. A textual critic asks simple questions. Which reading do the witnesses support? Which reading best explains how the others arose? Which errors do copyists usually make?

Deuteronomy 32:8 is a favorite example. In the Masoretic Text, the Song of Moses says that when the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, He set their borders according to the number of the children of Israel. In the Septuagint the last words are according to the number of the angels of God. A small Hebrew fragment from Qumran Cave 4 reads sons of God. Many scholars think sons of God is the older reading. It may have been changed because it seemed to speak of many divine beings, and the Greek translators may have softened it to angels.

Jewish tradition reads the received text. Rashi explains children of Israel as the seventy who went down to Egypt, matching the seventy nations of Genesis 10. The rabbinic reading and the historical reading are answering different questions: one asks what the verse means in the Torah as received, the other asks what the earliest copy said. A student in a public school can learn both and keep them straight.

A few working rules guide textual critics. The harder reading is often earlier, because copyists tend to smooth. The shorter reading is often earlier, because copyists tend to add. A reading that explains the others is preferred. None of these is a law; each case is weighed. For most of the Tanakh the witnesses agree, and the work concerns spelling. For a few hundred verses, the questions are real and open.

words.d: the study of manuscripts and versions to trace a text's transmission and its earliest recoverable form
the rule that the more difficult of two readings is often older, since copyists tend to smooth what puzzles them
the poem in Deuteronomy 32 that tradition ascribes to Moses at the end of his life

lessons.title: Bomberg's Bible and the Text Today
lessons.mainIdea: The printed Rabbinic Bible of 1525 fixed the Hebrew text for four centuries, and modern editions return to the great codices while keeping the Masoretic tradition.
reading: Printing reached the Hebrew Bible late in the fifteenth century, and the decisive edition came from Venice. Daniel Bomberg, a Christian printer from Antwerp, published a first Rabbinic Bible in 1517 and a second, far more careful, in 1524–25. Its editor was Jacob ben Hayyim ibn Adonijah, a Jewish scholar from Tunis, who gathered manuscripts and reconstructed the masorah from them. The *Rabbinic Bible* set the Hebrew text in the middle of the page with Targum Onkelos and the commentaries of Rashi, Ibn Ezra and others around it.

Ben Hayyim's text became the received text of the Hebrew Bible for the next four hundred years. Christian scholars used it too; the translators of the King James Version worked from editions descended from it. Its page layout became the model for the *Mikraot Gedolot*, the great rabbinic Bibles still printed today, in which a student reads the verse and a thousand years of commentary on one opening.

In the twentieth century editors went back behind Bomberg to the manuscripts. Biblia Hebraica in its third edition of 1937 and its successor, the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia of 1977, print the Leningrad Codex with notes on variants. The Hebrew University Bible Project in Jerusalem builds its edition on the Aleppo Codex. Israeli editions such as the Koren Tanakh and the Jerusalem Crown likewise follow the codices. The differences among all of these are small; the Masoretic tradition is one.

So the text today is a meeting point. A Torah scroll in a Chicago synagogue is written by a scribe following rules that go back through the Rabbinic Bible and the Masoretes. A scholar's edition prints the same consonants with a note wherever Qumran or the Greek differ. A translation committee sits between them. Jewish tradition holds the text it received; the history of that text is something anyone can study.

chapters.title: Translating the Tanakh
chapters.bigQuestion: If every translation is an interpretation, what does a reader gain and lose in moving from Hebrew to English, and who decides?

story.title: One Word, Six Choices
story.kicker: In a Philadelphia meeting room in the years before 1917, a committee of scholars argued over a single Hebrew word that English could not hold.
paragraphs: Picture a long table in Philadelphia, sometime between 1908 and 1915. Around it sit seven men: Max Margolis, the editor-in-chief, and six other scholars, rabbis and professors from different branches of American Jewish life. On the table are stacks of paper, a Hebrew Bible, the English Revised Version of 1885 and a pile of older Jewish translations. They are producing the first English Bible translated by a committee of Jews for the Jewish community in America.

The word on the table this afternoon is *chesed*. It appears about 250 times in the Tanakh. In Psalm 23 it walks with the reader. In Ruth it describes what a foreign widow does for her mother-in-law. In the prophets it is what God asks for instead of sacrifice. The English Revised Version, which the committee has agreed to take as its base, renders it in different places as mercy, kindness, lovingkindness, goodness and favour. Six English words for one Hebrew one.

One member wants a single English word every time, so that a reader can trace the thread. Another says no single word fits: mercy is too soft in Ruth and kindness is too small in the Psalms. A third says the committee's job is to render the Hebrew for Jewish readers, not to smooth it for English ears. The chairman notes that the Christian versions have already made their choices and asks what a Jewish translation owes to the Hebrew that they do not.

The debate above is imagined, but the questions were real, and the committee's answers stand in the 1917 text: the same word rendered differently as the context asks, with the Hebrew always in view. Every translator faces that table. This chapter sits at it with them, from Isaiah 7:14 to the name of God, and asks what a reader in a Chicago classroom should know about the English on the page.
story.think: Should a translation use one English word for one Hebrew word every time, or choose the best fit each time? What does each choice cost the reader?

lessons.title: What a Translation Does
lessons.mainIdea: A translation is a chain of decisions about words, grammar and sound, so no two translations of a verse say quite the same thing.
reading: Open the Tanakh in two English versions and the first sentence already differs. The King James Version of 1611 begins, In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, and so does the Jewish Publication Society version of 1917. But the New JPS of 1985 begins differently: When God began to create heaven and earth. The Hebrew is the same seven words. What changed is how the translators read the grammar of the first word, *bereshit*.

Rashi, in the eleventh century, had already argued that bereshit means in the beginning of, so that verse 1 is a clause leading into verse 2, not a complete sentence about a first act. The NJPS committee followed that reading of the grammar. The King James followed the older tradition, shared by the Septuagint, of a full sentence. Neither is a mistranslation. Each is an *interpretation* of ambiguous Hebrew, made in English where the reader cannot see the ambiguity.

That is the rule for every verse. The Hebrew has no capital letters, so a translator decides whether a word like spirit is a name. It has few punctuation marks of the modern kind, so a translator decides where a sentence ends. Its verbs mark aspect more than tense, so a translator decides whether an action is past or ongoing. Every such decision is a reading, and a reader who knows only English is reading the translator's reading.

words.d: the first Hebrew word of Genesis, rendered in the beginning (KJV, JPS 1917) or when God began (NJPS)
a reader's account of what a text means; every translation is one
what a verb form says about whether an action is complete or ongoing, which Hebrew marks more clearly than time

lessons.title: Isaiah 7:14 in Two Bibles
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah 7:14 shows how one Hebrew word, almah, became a dividing line between Jewish and Christian translations.
reading: In Isaiah 7 the prophet speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, who is frightened by two kings marching against Jerusalem, around 734 BCE. Isaiah offers a sign: a young woman is pregnant and will bear a son named Immanuel, God is with us, and before the child knows right from wrong the two kings will be gone. In its setting the sign is about the next few years of Ahaz's reign. The Hebrew word for the woman is *almah*, a young woman of marriageable age.

The Septuagint rendered almah with parthenos, a Greek word that usually means virgin. The Gospel of Matthew, quoting the Greek, read the verse as a prophecy of the birth of Jesus. From then on the verse belonged to two communities reading it two ways. Christian translations, from the Latin Vulgate to the King James, wrote virgin. Jewish readers, including Rashi, insisted the Hebrew says young woman and that the sign is about Ahaz's time.

The JPS 1917 committee, translating for Jews, wrote the young woman. The King James wrote a virgin. Neither committee was careless; each was faithful to a tradition of reading. In 1952 a Protestant translation, the Revised Standard Version, also wrote young woman, and some readers publicly burned copies in protest. That reaction shows what is at stake in a single word: not grammar only, but which community's reading a Bible will carry.

A public-school student does not have to decide who is right. What a student can do is state each reading accurately: the Hebrew word, what it means in the rest of the Tanakh, what the Greek did with it, and how Jewish and Christian readers have understood the verse since. That is the discipline this course asks for, and Isaiah 7:14 is the clearest place to practice it.

the name given to the child in Isaiah 7:14; Hebrew for God is with us

lessons.title: One Verse in Five Versions
lessons.mainIdea: Setting several translations of one verse side by side shows what each translator valued: tradition, sense, grammar or sound.
reading: Genesis 1:2 describes the earth before creation with a Hebrew phrase of two rhyming words, *tohu va-vohu*. The words are rare; tohu means emptiness or waste, and vohu appears only beside it. The King James wrote without form, and void, a phrase that entered English. JPS 1917 wrote unformed and void. NJPS 1985 kept unformed and void. Each of these gives the sense and lets the sound go.

Two modern translators went the other way. Robert Alter, in his translation completed in 2018, and Everett Fox, in The Five Books of Moses of 1995, each chose a pair of English words beginning with the same sound, so that an English reader hears the echo of the Hebrew pair. Their choices differ, but their aim is the same: to carry the poetry, not only the meaning. A reader who compares all five learns something no single version can teach.

This is why serious study uses more than one translation. The course text is JPS 1917, because it is a Jewish translation in the public domain, and because its English, close to the King James, lets a student hear the older tradition. Beside it a student can set NJPS for clearer sense, Alter or Fox for sound, and the King James to see what English literature inherited. Where they agree, the Hebrew is plain. Where they differ, there is something to learn.

None of this makes translation hopeless. Most verses of the Tanakh are narrative and law, and their sense crosses into English well. The hard cases are poetry, wordplay, and a small set of words that hold whole ideas. The rest of this chapter looks at those words, and at the people who have sat at the translator's table.

an American literary scholar whose translation of the whole Hebrew Bible, attentive to its sound and style, was completed in 2018
an American scholar whose The Five Books of Moses (1995) follows the Buber–Rosenzweig method of echoing the Hebrew sound
works whose copyright has expired, such as JPS 1917 and the King James, which anyone may quote freely

look.title: Which Translation for Which Reader?
look.text: Five readers want a copy of Genesis. A synagogue Hebrew-school class wants a Jewish translation that is clear on first reading. A high-school English teacher wants the version Milton and Lincoln knew. A poet wants to hear the rhythm of the Hebrew. A rabbi preparing a sermon wants the sense modern scholars agree on. A student in this course wants a Jewish translation anyone can quote without permission.
look.prompt: Match each reader to one of these: King James, JPS 1917, NJPS 1985, Alter, Fox. Give a reason for each match. Is there a reader for whom two versions would be better than one?

check.q: How do Alter and Fox handle tohu va-vohu differently from JPS 1917?
choices: They choose English words that echo the Hebrew sound
They translate it as without form, and void
They omit the phrase as untranslatable
check.why: Alter and Fox each choose a pair of alliterating English words to carry the sound of the Hebrew pair; JPS 1917 gives the sense as unformed and void.

check.q: Why is JPS 1917 the text of this course?
choices: It is the newest Jewish translation
It is the only translation Jews accept
It is a Jewish translation in the public domain with English close to the King James
check.why: JPS 1917 is a Jewish translation whose copyright has expired, and its older English lets students hear the tradition the King James shaped.

check.q: What kind of passage is hardest to translate, according to the lesson?
choices: Poetry, wordplay and a few words that hold whole ideas
check.why: Narrative and law cross into English well; poetry, puns and key terms like chesed are where translations diverge most.

lessons.title: The 1917 Committee
lessons.mainIdea: The JPS 1917 translation was the first English Bible produced by a committee of Jewish scholars for American Jews, built on the Revised Version and the Hebrew.
reading: The Jewish Publication Society was founded in Philadelphia in 1888 to publish Jewish books in English. American Jews had used Isaac Leeser's translation of 1853, the work of one man. Or they used Christian Bibles, with the Christian order of books and Christian readings of verses like Isaiah 7:14. The Society decided a new translation was needed. After a first attempt book by book, it appointed a committee in 1908.

The editor-in-chief was *Max Margolis*, a Hebrew scholar born in Lithuania who taught at Dropsie College in Philadelphia. The committee of six who reviewed his drafts included rabbis and professors from Reform and traditional backgrounds, and Cyrus Adler chaired its board. They agreed to take the English Revised Version of 1885 as their base, keeping its language where it matched the Hebrew and revising wherever Jewish tradition or the Hebrew required. The work took seven years and appeared in 1917.

The result reads much like the King James: thee and thou, shall and hath. But it follows the Tanakh's order and its 24 books, ends with Chronicles, uses the Hebrew verse numbering, renders almah as young woman, and consults Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Kimchi throughout. Its preface says the translators aimed to combine the spirit of Jewish tradition with the results of biblical scholarship. For most of the twentieth century it was the English Bible of American synagogues, and it remains in print and freely available.

words.d: the Philadelphia publisher, founded 1888, that produced the 1917 and 1985 English translations of the Tanakh
the Lithuanian-born Hebrew scholar who served as editor-in-chief of the JPS 1917 translation
the British revision of the King James, completed in 1885, that the JPS 1917 committee used as its English base
the Philadelphia rabbi whose 1853 translation was the main Jewish English Bible before 1917

look.title: A Century of Jewish English Bibles
rows: Fox, The Five Books of Moses
look.cite: Publication dates as given by the Jewish Publication Society, Schocken Books and W. W. Norton
look.prompt: How many years passed between the two JPS translations? What had changed in American Jewish life and in biblical scholarship that might explain why a new one was wanted?

check.q: What English text did the JPS 1917 committee use as its base?
check.why: The committee took the Revised Version as its base, revising it toward the Hebrew and Jewish tradition.

check.q: Who was the editor-in-chief of the 1917 translation?
check.why: Margolis prepared the drafts; Adler chaired the board; Leeser translated in 1853; Orlinsky led the NJPS Torah decades later.

check.q: Which of these is a way JPS 1917 differs from the King James?
choices: It follows the Tanakh's order and ends with Chronicles
It is written in modern English
It omits the book of Esther
It includes the books of Maccabees

lessons.title: The New JPS of 1985
lessons.mainIdea: The NJPS translation, completed in 1985, replaced the old English with modern prose and translated by sense rather than word for word.
reading: By the 1950s the 1917 English sounded old, and scholarship on Hebrew had moved. The Jewish Publication Society began a new translation. The Torah appeared in 1962 under Harry Orlinsky, a professor who had also served on the Protestant Revised Standard Version committee, the only Jewish scholar to do so. The Prophets followed in 1978 and the Writings in 1982, and the whole appeared as one volume in 1985, the *NJPS*, or New JPS Tanakh.

The committee's method was different. Where 1917 kept the word order and rhythm of the older English, NJPS aimed at *idiomatic* English, translating the sense of a Hebrew sentence into the sentence an English writer would use. Thee and thou are gone. Where the Hebrew is uncertain, a footnote says Meaning of Hebrew uncertain. Where the Hebrew can be read two ways, a footnote gives the other. Rashi and the medieval commentators are consulted, but so is the study of related languages such as Ugaritic and Akkadian.

The gains are clarity and honesty about doubt. The costs are the ones every idiomatic translation pays: the reader cannot see the Hebrew word order, repeated words are sometimes varied for English style, and a phrase that once echoed the King James no longer does. NJPS is the translation printed in most American non-Orthodox synagogue Bibles today. Because it is under copyright, this course describes it but quotes only JPS 1917.

words.d: the New Jewish Publication Society translation, published in parts from 1962 and complete in 1985
the scholar who led the NJPS Torah (1962) and served on the Protestant Revised Standard Version committee
translated into the natural phrasing of the target language, sense for sense rather than word for word
a translator's note at the foot of the page, used by NJPS to flag uncertain Hebrew or another possible reading

look.title: Word for Word or Sense for Sense?
look.text: Two translators face a Hebrew sentence that says, literally, and he lifted up his eyes and saw. The first writes exactly that, because that is the Hebrew idiom and it appears many times. The second writes he looked up and saw, because that is what an English writer would say and the meaning is the same. Later in the story the phrase appears again at a turning point, and the reader of the second translation cannot tell it is the same phrase.
look.prompt: Which translator would you want for a first reading? Which for a close study of the story's repeated phrases? Can a footnote solve the problem, or does it just move it?

check.q: When was the complete NJPS Tanakh published?
check.why: The Torah appeared in 1962 and the full NJPS in 1985; 1917 is the older JPS and 1995 is Fox's Five Books.

check.q: What does idiomatic translation mean?
choices: Rendering the sense in natural English phrasing
Translating only idioms and leaving the rest
check.why: Idiomatic translation gives the meaning in the sentence an English writer would use, which is the NJPS method.

check.q: How does NJPS handle a Hebrew phrase whose meaning is unclear?
choices: It always follows the King James
It translates and adds a footnote saying the meaning is uncertain
check.why: NJPS is known for its footnotes, including Meaning of Hebrew uncertain and notes giving other possible readings.

lessons.title: Buber, Rosenzweig and Fox
lessons.mainIdea: Martin Buber and Franz Rosenzweig translated the Bible into German to be heard aloud, and Everett Fox carried their method into English.
reading: In 1925 two German-Jewish thinkers, *Martin Buber* and *Franz Rosenzweig*, began a new translation of the Hebrew Bible into German. They believed that the Bible was meant to be spoken and heard. Earlier translations, including Luther's, had in their view smoothed it into good German prose and lost the Hebrew's voice. Their aim was to make German do what Hebrew does. Keep the word order. Keep repeated words repeated. Break the text into breath-units, lines the length of a spoken phrase.

Rosenzweig, already ill, died in 1929 with the work at Isaiah. Buber continued alone, through his emigration to Jerusalem in 1938 and the destruction of the German-Jewish world for which the translation had been made, and finished it in 1961. He called the completed work Die Schrift, the Scripture. Readers still find it strange and powerful: German that sounds like Hebrew.

*Everett Fox*, an American scholar, applied the same principles to English. His The Five Books of Moses appeared in 1995, followed by The Early Prophets in 2014. Fox prints the text in lines, not paragraphs, keeps Hebrew names in Hebrew form, so Moses is Moshe and Isaac is Yitzhak, and lets a Hebrew word that repeats ten times repeat ten times in English. His translations are used in classrooms where teachers want students to hear the text's structure.

The Buber–Rosenzweig–Fox approach is one answer to the question this chapter keeps asking. If translation must lose something, what should it keep? JPS 1917 kept the tradition of English Bibles. NJPS kept the sense. Buber, Rosenzweig and Fox kept the sound and the shape. A reader can hold all three answers and choose the one the moment needs.

words.d: the German-Jewish philosopher (1878–1965) who, with Rosenzweig, translated the Bible into German, finishing alone in 1961
the German-Jewish thinker (1886–1929) who began the Bible translation with Buber and died with it unfinished
the Scripture: the title of the completed Buber–Rosenzweig German Bible
a line of text the length of a spoken phrase, the unit Buber, Rosenzweig and Fox use to lay out the Bible

look.title: Moshe or Moses?
look.text: Fox writes Moshe where JPS 1917 writes Moses, and Yitzhak where it writes Isaac. The English names come through Greek and Latin and are the ones English readers know from art, literature and everyday speech. The Hebrew names are the ones Jewish readers use in synagogue and the ones that carry the puns the Torah makes on them: Yitzhak echoes the Hebrew for laughter, which the story of his birth turns on.
look.prompt: What does a reader gain from Yitzhak, and what does a reader lose? Should a translation for a public-school class use one, the other, or both?

check.q: What was the main aim of the Buber–Rosenzweig translation?
choices: To make German that keeps the Hebrew's sound, word order and repetitions
To produce the first German Bible
To translate the Septuagint into German
check.why: Buber and Rosenzweig wanted German to be heard the way Hebrew is heard, keeping repeated words and breath-length lines.

check.q: Who completed Die Schrift, and when?
check.why: Rosenzweig died in 1929; Buber finished the translation alone in Jerusalem in 1961.

check.q: Which of these is a feature of Everett Fox's translation?
choices: Footnotes reading Meaning of Hebrew uncertain
Hebrew forms of names such as Moshe and Yitzhak
check.why: Fox keeps Hebrew name forms and line breaks; the footnote phrase belongs to NJPS and thee and thou to JPS 1917.

lessons.title: Chesed and Tzedek
lessons.mainIdea: Chesed and tzedek each hold a cluster of English meanings, so translators must choose one and readers must remember the rest.
reading: *Chesed* is one of the most frequent words in the Tanakh's poetry and one of the hardest to carry into English. It names loyal, active kindness inside a relationship: what a person does for family, ally or covenant partner because of the bond between them. Ruth's care for Naomi is chesed. God's steadfast love for Israel in the Psalms is chesed. The prophet Hosea says God desires chesed and not sacrifice. JPS 1917 renders it mercy, kindness or lovingkindness as the verse seems to ask.

*Tzedek*, with its relative *tzedakah*, names what is right: justice in a court, fairness in weights and measures, righteousness in a person. In later Hebrew tzedakah came to mean giving to the poor, since the rabbis saw such giving as justice owed, not charity offered. English splits the idea. Justice sounds like courts; righteousness sounds like personal goodness. The Hebrew holds both in one word, so a verse about tzedek in the market is also a verse about tzedek before God.

Micah 6:8 puts the two words side by side. The prophet asks what the LORD requires and answers, as JPS 1917 has it, to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God. In Hebrew the second phrase is to love chesed. A reader of the English sees mercy and may think of pardon. A reader of the Hebrew hears the whole cluster: loyalty, kindness, the duty of a bond. That is why a study Bible glosses the word, and why this course teaches it.

words.d: loyal, active kindness within a bond; rendered mercy, kindness or lovingkindness in JPS 1917
justice, rightness, righteousness: what is right in a court, a market or a life
righteousness; in later Hebrew, giving to the poor understood as justice owed rather than charity
a short explanation of a word placed beside it, in a margin, a note or a bracket

look.title: What the LORD Requires
look.text: It has been told to you, human being, what is good and what the LORD asks of you: only to do justice, to love chesed, and to walk humbly with your God.
look.cite: Micah 6:8, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), with the Hebrew word chesed retained
look.prompt: Replace chesed in turn with mercy, kindness and loyal love. How does the verse's demand change with each? Which English word would you choose, and what would you write in a footnote?

check.q: Which of these is the best description of chesed?
choices: Loyal, active kindness within a relationship or covenant
check.why: Chesed names kindness that flows from a bond, as in Ruth's care for Naomi or God's steadfast love in the Psalms.

check.q: How did the meaning of tzedakah shift in later Hebrew?
choices: From giving to the poor to courtroom justice
From righteousness to giving to the poor, seen as justice owed
From a person's name to a common noun
check.why: The rabbis understood giving to the poor as an act of justice, so tzedakah became the word for such giving.

check.q: At Micah 6:8, what Hebrew word does JPS 1917 render as mercy?
check.why: The phrase to love mercy renders to love chesed; to do justly renders the word for justice, mishpat.

lessons.title: Nefesh, Ruach and Shalom
lessons.mainIdea: Nefesh, ruach and shalom are body-and-life words that English tends to make spiritual or narrow, and translators must resist both.
reading: In Genesis 2:7, as JPS 1917 tells it, God forms the human from the dust, breathes into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human becomes a living *nefesh*. The 1917 English says living soul, following the King James. But nefesh in the Tanakh is not a soul separate from a body. It is the living being itself, the throat that breathes and hungers, the self. Animals are nefesh too in Genesis 1. Later English translations often write living being for that reason.

*Ruach* means wind, breath and spirit, and the Hebrew does not choose among them. In Genesis 1:2 a ruach of God moves over the waters: the King James wrote Spirit of God, JPS 1917 wrote spirit of God with a small s, and NJPS wrote a wind from God. Each is a reading. In Ezekiel 37 the prophet calls to the ruach to breathe into the dry bones, and the chapter plays on all three senses at once, wind, breath and spirit, in a way no English can follow without a note.

*Shalom* is usually translated peace, and peace is not wrong. But the Hebrew root means wholeness and completeness. To ask after someone's shalom is to ask how they are; to pay shalom, in Exodus 21 and 22, is to make restitution in full. Peace in English suggests the absence of war or of noise. Shalom in Hebrew suggests the presence of everything that should be there. A reader who keeps that in mind hears the greeting shalom, and the prayer for shalom in the synagogue, differently.

words.d: a living being, the self, the throat that breathes and hungers; living soul in JPS 1917 at Genesis 2:7
wind, breath or spirit; the Hebrew does not separate the three
peace, wholeness, well-being; also, in law, full restitution
making good a loss, paying back in full what was taken or damaged

look.title: Dust, Breath and a Living Being
look.text: Then the LORD God formed the human of dust from the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and the human became a living nefesh.
look.cite: Genesis 2:7, paraphrased from the Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), with the Hebrew word nefesh retained
look.prompt: JPS 1917 and the King James write living soul; several later translations write living being. What does each English choice suggest about what a person is? Which fits Genesis 1, where animals are also called nefesh?

check.q: In the Tanakh, what does nefesh most often mean?
choices: A soul that lives apart from the body
The living being or self, including its breath and hunger
check.why: Nefesh is the living creature itself, which is why animals are called nefesh in Genesis 1 and why some translations write living being.

check.q: How do the King James and NJPS differ at the ruach of Genesis 1:2?
choices: KJV Spirit of God; NJPS a wind from God
KJV a wind from God; NJPS Spirit of God
check.why: The King James writes Spirit of God; NJPS chose wind from God; JPS 1917 kept spirit with a small s. Each reads the same Hebrew word.

check.q: What does the root of shalom mean beyond peace?
check.why: Shalom's root is wholeness; in Exodus 21–22 the verb means to pay in full, and the greeting asks after a person's well-being.

lessons.title: Torah: Law or Teaching?
lessons.mainIdea: Torah means teaching or instruction, and translating it as law, following the Greek nomos, has shaped how outsiders picture Judaism.
reading: The word *torah* comes from a Hebrew root meaning to point out or to teach. In the Tanakh it can mean a single rule, a body of instruction, or the whole teaching of Moses. Proverbs speaks of the torah of a mother. Psalm 19 praises the torah of the LORD as perfect, restoring the soul. In later Jewish usage Torah means the five books, and then the whole of Jewish teaching, written and oral.

The Septuagint translated torah with the Greek *nomos*, law, and the Latin and English Bibles followed: the law of the LORD, the law of Moses. Law is not wrong; much of the Torah is law. But law in English suggests courts, penalties and a code, and the word carried into Christian writing a picture of Judaism as a religion of rules against a religion of grace. Jewish scholars from the nineteenth century on have pointed out that torah as teaching, instruction and way is closer to what the word does in Hebrew.

JPS 1917 still writes law, following the older English. NJPS often writes teaching, and its Psalm 19 has the teaching of the LORD is perfect. Alter and Fox make similar choices. A student who reads law in the course text can hold the Hebrew in mind, and can notice that Jewish tradition itself calls the study of these books not law school but Torah study, learning. The word chosen in translation shapes the image of a whole tradition; that is the largest reason translation matters.

The same lesson applies to *mitzvah*, commandment, which in Jewish life also means a good deed done because it is commanded, and to *brit*, covenant, which JPS 1917 renders covenant every time but which English readers may hear as a mere contract. In each case the translator can only choose a word. The reader must learn the rest.

words.d: teaching or instruction; the five books of Moses; the whole of Jewish teaching. Rendered law in JPS 1917 and the King James
the Greek word for law that the Septuagint used for torah, from which English law descends
a commandment; in Jewish life also a good deed done because it is commanded
covenant, the binding bond between God and Israel in the Tanakh; more than a contract

look.title: The Law of the LORD Is Perfect

The Hebrew word is torah in both. Read the two lines aloud. One sounds like a statute; the other like a lesson. The psalm goes on to compare the word to honey and to gold.

check.why: Nomos, law, is the Septuagint's regular rendering; parthenos belongs to Isaiah 7:14 and logos and sophia are other words entirely.

check.why: NJPS writes the teaching of the LORD, while JPS 1917 keeps the older law.

lessons.title: The Name of God
lessons.mainIdea: Jews do not pronounce the four-letter name of God, and translations from the Septuagint to JPS 1917 have rendered it the LORD rather than transliterating it.
reading: In Exodus 3, at the burning bush, Moses asks what he should say when the Israelites ask the name of the God who sent him. The answer, as JPS 1917 has it, is I AM THAT I AM, and then a four-letter name related to the Hebrew verb to be. That name appears more than six thousand times in the Tanakh, more often than any other name. It is written in every Torah scroll. And for at least two thousand years Jews have not said it aloud.

Jewish tradition holds that the name was pronounced only by the high priest in the Temple on Yom Kippur. After the Temple's destruction the pronunciation was no longer taught, and the Mishnah lists one who pronounces the name as written among those who forfeit their share in the world to come. In reading, Jews substitute *Adonai*, my Lord, and in ordinary speech many say *HaShem*, the Name. The Masoretes marked the four letters with the vowels of the substitute word as a reminder. Some Jews extend the care to English and write G-d.

Translations followed the reading, not the writing. The Septuagint wrote Kyrios, Lord. The King James wrote the LORD in small capitals wherever the four letters stand, and Lord in ordinary type where the Hebrew says Adonai. JPS 1917 kept that convention, and this course does too. NJPS keeps the LORD as well. A few Christian and scholarly versions transliterate the name with vowels; Jewish translations do not, and Fox writes YHWH, the four consonants alone, so that a reader sees a name and says the substitute.

For a student, the practical rule is simple. When the English says the LORD in capitals, the Hebrew has the four-letter name; when it says God, the Hebrew usually has *Elohim*; when it says Lord, the Hebrew has Adonai. Knowing that, a reader of JPS 1917 can see which name a passage uses. That matters in Genesis, where scholars have long noticed that some passages prefer one name and some the other.

words.d: my Lord: the word Jews read aloud in place of the four-letter name
the Name: how many Jews refer to God in ordinary speech
the Hebrew word for God, rendered God in JPS 1917
the typographic form the LORD, used by the King James and JPS 1917 wherever the Hebrew has the four-letter name

look.prompt: The name is tied to a verb, not a noun. What might it mean for a name to be a form of to be? Why might a tradition decide that such a name is not to be spoken?

choices: They spell out the four letters
check.why: The reading tradition substitutes Adonai; in everyday speech many say HaShem, the Name.

check.q: How does JPS 1917 show that the Hebrew has the four-letter name?
choices: It prints the LORD in small capitals
check.why: Following the King James convention, JPS 1917 writes the LORD in small capitals for the name and Lord for Adonai.

check.q: According to Jewish tradition, who alone pronounced the name, and when?
choices: The high priest in the Temple on Yom Kippur

lessons.title: Who Translates, for Whom
lessons.mainIdea: Every translation is made by particular people for particular readers, and knowing who and for whom is part of reading it well.
reading: Ask three questions of any Bible on a shelf. Who made it? For whom? Why? The King James was made by about fifty Church of England scholars for the English church and crown in 1611, and it reads Christian theology into some verses of the Tanakh. JPS 1917 was made by a committee of American Jews for American synagogues. NJPS was made by Jewish scholars for a community that wanted modern English and modern scholarship. Fox translated for readers who want to hear the Hebrew. None of these is neutral; each is honest about its purpose.

Who is at the table matters in other ways. Until the twentieth century almost every published Bible translator was a man; the JPS committees of 1908 and the 1960s had no women. Recent Jewish translations and commentaries have changed that, and some, such as the 2006 Contemporary Torah from JPS, revisit the rendering of gendered language about people and about God. Whether such changes are faithful or unfaithful is debated inside Jewish communities, as it is inside Christian ones. A student can report the debate without joining it.

For whom also shapes the page. A synagogue Bible prints the Hebrew and English facing each other, with the weekly readings marked. A scholar's edition prints notes on variants. A children's Bible retells. An interfaith edition may print Jewish and Christian readings of a verse side by side. In Chicago, a student can find all of these within a few miles: in synagogue libraries, at the Newberry Library, at the university libraries, and in the Spertus Institute's collection.

So the last skill of this unit is a habit. When you read a verse in English, ask which translation it is, when it was made, and by whom; check the Hebrew word if it matters; and, where readers differ, say who reads it which way. That habit is not suspicion. It is what respect for a text looks like when the text has been translated for two thousand years.

words.d: a person or committee who renders a text from one language into another, always making choices
words that mark a person or being as male or female, such as he, man or father, which translators must decide how to render
involving more than one religious tradition, as when an edition prints Jewish and Christian readings together
